short: The sack that killed the last Abbasid caliph and ended five centuries of rule from Baghdad.
full:
Hulagu Khan demanded that al-Musta'sim dismantle his walls and send troops to serve the Mongols. The caliph, thirty-seventh of his line and advised that the Muslim world would rise if Baghdad were touched, refused. Mongol columns closed on the city from both banks of the Tigris and broke a sortie by trapping it against ground they had flooded by cutting the dykes. The siege began on 29 January 1258; by 5 February the eastern wall was in Mongol hands, and the city surrendered on 10 February.

The sack lasted a week. Estimates of the dead run from tens of thousands to 800,000 and none are reliable; the libraries, including the House of Wisdom, were destroyed, and chroniclers wrote of the Tigris running black with ink. Al-Musta'sim was executed on 20 February, by tradition rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses. Hulagu's Nestorian Christian wife Doquz Khatun obtained protection for the city's Christians. The Abbasid caliphate survived only as a title held by refugees under Mamluk protection in Cairo.
